#4642. The 92 Best Movies of 2026 So Far (and 13 More We Can't Wait For)

With Christopher Nolan, star-studded epic romance, and major Marvel events, this list is a behemoth. And it also features a movie called Behomoth!.

AS A HUGE fan and follower of both movies and sports, the former has one major advantage: There's always something to look forward to. As a fan of the New York Jets, I don't always have that luxury. As a fan of watching films, though, not only is there always something worth my time on the big screen or streaming, but there's always several flicks down the line that will sound great or intriguing for one reason or another. Will they all turn out great? Of course not. But with sports and movies alike, excitement tends to be all about hope.

After a particularly strong 2025—movies like One Battle After Another and Sinners proved to be true standouts—how does 2026 pick up? With strength and energy, that's how. The year has been filled with all sorts of great movies, from horror (like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Obsession) to epics (like The Odyssey), to some pretty great comedies (like Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie and The Invite). It’s been a good year.

But we always like to look at not only what’s been good to date, but also what we can still be excited for—and that includes everything. We’re talking stuff on the calendar already, stuff we suspect could come out this year, and even stuff making noise in places like the Sundance Film Festival. Throughout the year, this list evolves from our most anticpated movies into our favorite movies, and always looks quite different in December than it did in January.

For now, we've got a lot we’ve loved, but still a lot to look forward to as well. Below, we've listed nearly 100 movies on our radar that we think you'll be really interested in seeing.

If you're interested in a killer chimpanzee B-movie slasher, then Primate is for you. The movie delivers what it promises. Ben the chimpanzee does some very terrible things on screen but it makes for quite an enjoyable experience.

28 Years Later: The Bone Temple is a direct sequel to last year's 28 Years Later. And while the great Danny Boyle doesn't return to direct, the movie is helmed by the more-than-capable Nia DaCosta and once again counts Alex Garland as its screenwriter. The real assets, though, are the movie's leads: Ralph Fiennes and Jack O'Connell are sensational, magnetic every minute they're on screen amidst all sorts of post-apocalyptic chaos. Bring on part three.

Here's a quick pitch for The Rip: Matt Damon and Ben Affleck. The longtime friends team up once again for The Rip, a cop thriller in the vein of movies you've probably seen several times before... but done particularly well. This twisty crime story involves a police team finding a ton of money in a stash house (the titular rip), and figuring out who may or may not be corrupt. In addition to our beloved duo, the cast is shockingly stacked: Steven Yeun, Kyle Chandler, Scott Adkins, and One Battle After AnotherAcademy Award nominee Teyana Taylor are all on board.

SAM RAIMI FANS, ASSEMBLE! For the first time since 2009, the master of gross effects and frenetic cameras is back with an original horror story in Send Help. Rachel McAdams plays a Survivor superfan who gets stuck on an island with her dickhead boss (Dylan O'Brien), and then the antics begin. Think Cast Away meets Misery meets Drag Me to Hell. It's great stuff.

Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista are a pair of cool dudes who, with The Wrecking Crew, set out and did exactly what they intended to do: Make a badass buddy action comedy. The movie finds the pair playing estranged brothers who reunite in Hawaii to investigate their father's mysterious death; From there, we get lots of jokes, and a lot of (very violent!!!) action. It's a good time! Honestly, if they want to make a couple sequels to this, I'd be her for it.

Part This Is Spinal Tap, part Josie and the Pussycats, and part Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Moment is Charli XCX's movie for anyone who enjoys her music, persona, or both. A really fun movie about music, stardom, and celebrity in 2026.

Pillion was technically released initially in 2025 (and was also included on our list of favorite movies of that year), but we didn't want to miss an opportunity to recommend it to people once again. This unique film follows a man (Harry Melling) who engages in an unexpected BDSM relationship with a biker he meets at random (Alexander Skarsgård). The movie is quite the tonal balancing act, at times funny, intense, raunchy, and heartbreaking, but it all comes together by the end. A delightful movie, and a great showcase for both leads.

The classic novel comes to life on the big screen once again, this time from Promising Young Woman and Saltburn director Emerald Fennell, and with Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi in the lead roles. Fennell, an Academy Award winner for her work on Promising Young Woman, has both big fans and big detractors at this point—but her take her, while book purists haven't been thrilled, is a big, visually stunning epic romance. Robbie and Elordi are both up to the task as well, bringing a charged energy to roles that really need it. Alison Oliver, who recently shined on HBO's Task, is another major highlight in a supporting role. An original soundtrack from Charli XCX helps to set the anachronistic mood and feels like a real cherry on top.

This action-thriller, based on a book by Don Winslow, looks like a very solid entry in the genre that we're going to call "Somewhat Resembles a Michael Mann Film." And reviews have confirmed as much—the movie has often been compared to Heat, and while its tough to compare to Mann's 1995 masterpiece, we'll take just about anything in that vein. Look: If someone tells you there's gonna be a crime thriller in the vein of Heat with Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Halle Berry, and Barry Keoghan leading the cast, how could you not be on board?

One of our coolest directors, Gore Verbinski, makes his grand return with Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die—his first movie since 2016's A Cure For Wellness. If you don't know Verbinski by name, you should know several of his movies: the original Pirates of the Caribbean trilogy, The Ring, and Rango are among the standouts. Good Luck follows Sam Rockwell as a man who claims to be from the future and fighting off a rogue artificial intelligence. While the movie takes some pretty tough and labored tangents into on-the-nose satire, Rockwell's performance and the practical effects keep the movie afloat as a fun sci-fi romp.

Despite the title, you don't need to know anything else about Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie before going to see it. Sure, this story of two inept dudes in a band who just want to play music at a bar—and go through all sorts of ordeals, including time-travel, to do it—has existed before in both web series and television series form. But you can just go in and laugh and the absolute madness of the movie. Trust us—you'll have a good time with this one if you're into "madness that makes you laugh." This is a long-term passion project of Matt Johnson, who became well known recently for directing the underrated BlackBerry. His brash talent is again on display here.

We're always in on Glen Powell, and How to Make a Killing marks his first foray into A24's world as a leading man. This black comedy neo-noir comes from Emily the Criminal director John Patton Ford and follows Powell as a man who decides to take out a few members of his family in order to increase his chance at making a whole bunch of money via inheritance. The supporting cast joining Powell isn't too shabby: Margaret Qualley, Jessica Henwick, Ed Harris, and Topher Grace are all along for the fun.

The Napa Boys is a very specific cut for comedy fans. Remember when all those nondescript American Pie direct-to-video sequels were coming out? "American Pie Presents:.."? The Napa Boys imagines itself as one of those: self-impressed raunchy comedy with little tact—crossed, naturally with the wine bro nature of 2004's Sideways. As a result, we get a movie that presents as a sequel to a franchise that both has long been running out of juice, and, in our world, never was. If you get the truly absurd brand of parody being presented here, you're going to get a real kick out of it.

Hoppers feels like a throwback to the golden age of Pixar. Not only is it an original story (at a time when the legendary animation studio has often been leaning into sequels, prequels, and more), but it's a sweet and funny one at that. Following an animal-lover who uses Avatar-style technology to transfer her consciousness into a robotic beaver body that can discover what animals are thinking and saying, Hoppers actually turns into something of a conspiracy mystery story. With a voice cast that includes Jon Hamm, Dave Franco, and Meryl Streep among others, it's a fun one for the whole family.

Look. This is one of those movies that you really don't have to overthink. It's Alan Ritchson—Reacher himself—taking on a giant alien robot monster thing. This is as much of a throwback to '80s-style action filmmaking as we're ever going to get, and it delivers as promised. The fact that the rest of the cast includes staples like Jai Courtney, Esai Morales, and Dennis Quaid is just a bonus.

Undertone has been positioning itself as A24's next huge horror hit—and we'll see how it lands. The filmfollows a supernatural podcaster who gets sent some particularly spooky recordings; Its soundscape has brought tons of hype, with many calling it the scariest experience of the year. A simple premise like that sometimes makes for a very solid horror movie.

Based on the novel by Andy Weir(who also wrote The Martian), Project Hail Mary is a story of space exploration and a regular guy (played by Ryan Gosling) who gets involved. Phil Lord and Chris Miller (who are responsible for the Spider-Verse movies and directed 21 Jump Street) are behind the camera for this one, which has already proven to be a big, big hit. Gosling is basically on his own out in space for most of this, but it also includes a fun little alien guy named Rocky and a nice supporting performance by Anatomy of a Fall star Sandra Hüller. The visuals here are worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find.

2018's Ready or Not was one of the most fun horror films of the last decade, and now eight years later we get to see Samara Weaving's lead sucked back into the same twisted, bloody, violent games. The supporting cast—including David Cronenberg (!!!), March MH Flex star Elijah Wood, Sarah Michelle Gellar, and The Pitt's Shawn Hatosy—is fantastic. The movie kind of keeps with the form of the first Ready or Not, so if you liked that one, you'll certainly have a fun time with this one.

Forbidden Fruits follows a secret coven of witches operating in a shopping mall. Like, guys, some premises you just have to accept for how good they are and see them out. The movie is a campy, fun, twisty turny ride. Understand what you're getting into—a little bit of horror, a little bit of satire, and some fun twists—and it's going to be a good time.

Zazie Beetz (Atlanta, Deadpool 2) gets to lead her own horror/thriller movie with They Will Kill You, where she plays a woman who answers a help-wanted ad for a housekeeper in a luxury apartment building, only to find herself fighting for her life. The movie is pretty similar in tone to fellow horror/comedy Ready or Not 2, which we just talked about. But They Will Kill You leans more into its John Wick-style action and Kill Bill style plot, which sets it apart. The supporting cast, which includes Patricia Arquette, Heather Graham, and Industry star Myha'la, make it extra worth it.

#4641. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4640. Volkswagen’s new electric SUV is taking over where the ID.4 left off

Volkswagen is turning one of its best-selling nameplates into an electric SUV. The new ID. Tiguan is now rolling off the assembly line and will replace the ID.4 in 2027.

The ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the new ID. Tiguan will replace them in Volkswagen’s EV lineup next year.

Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID. Tiguan is the next model to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the company calls it.

The new electric SUV adopts Volkswagen’s best-selling nameplate, the Tiguan, as part of its shift away from the numerical system used on the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5.

Volkswagen announced on Thursday that series production of the electric ID. Tiguan has now begun at its Embden Plant in Germany.

“The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer said last month after unveiling the new SUV. He added that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”

The ID. Tiguan will be a step change from its predecessors, the ID.4 and ID.5, featuring Volkswagen’s “Pure Positive” design language, which includes an overhauled interior and exterior design and updated tech.

Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan’s “hallmark feature” is the completely redesigned exterior. The new design remains closer to the gas-powered Tiguan, with a boxy, traditional SUV look.

Unlike the ID.4’s aerodynamic design, the new ID. Tiguan features a wide, chunky front end and traditional pull-style door handles instead of the flush ones.

In Volkswagen’s words, the new ID. Tiguan electric SUV “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment.”

Inside, the updates are just as evident. The overhauled interior features Volkswagen’s new infotainment setup, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and a 15″ center display. There’s also an optional 12″ passenger screen available.

Another highlight is the return of physical buttons. After listening to customer feedback from current drivers, Volkswagen added physical buttons under the center display and on the steering wheel for climate control and other vehicle functions.

To spark a bit of nostalgia, VW added a fun new Retro Mode feature that transforms the Digital Cockpit and center display to mimic the style of iconic models like the first-generation Golf.

Drivers can also choose from six classic VW models to display in a virtual “garage” on the infotainment screen: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg, and Beetle.

The new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:

Depending on the configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a “new benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe with a WLTP range of up to 377 miles (607 km).

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Tiguan in Germany and a few other European markets in October, starting at €42,695 ($47,800). It’s available in three trims: Trend, Life, and Style.

After it launches in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in North America to replace the ID.4.

Apparently, the new ID Tiguan has a slightly better Cx (Drag Coefficient) at 0.26 versus 0.28 on first gen ID4 and 0.27 on 2nd gen. According to VW, it’s achieved using front air curtains, a minimal air intake, an enclosed underbody, and a longer roof spoiler.

Volkswagen said prices and other details will come in “due course.” The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.

Since the European model offers close to 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.

Official US prices have not yet been announced. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of about $45,000, so the ID. Tiguan will likely be priced similarly.

#4639. ‘I Started Strength Training at 74. At 78, I Can Deadlift 132 Lbs—Here’s How.’

“While I love lifting weights and hitting new PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.”

If there’s one thing I’ve learned as I’ve gotten older, it’s that being active and being strong aren’t necessarily the same thing. For most of my life, I’d been recreationally active, and had loved kayaking, swimming, and taking my dog on long walks. I’d never done any kind of structured strength training, until right before my 75th birthday. One day, I was sitting on a curb outside my house, and when it was time to stand up, I couldn’t. I felt embarrassed, and the idea of falling and not being able to get up or being in a situation where I couldn’t take care of myself was scary.

I wanted everyday activities, like climbing stairs, carrying groceries, and getting up off the floor, to feel easier. I also wanted to trust my body more, and feel confident in my ability to handle whatever life threw my way. So, I joined Aspire Athletic Club, a gym near my home in Schenectady, New York, and began working out once a week with the owner, Chris Wertman. In the beginning, even simple movements were challenging, so I started with basic bodyweight exercises like the box squat, step-up, and bird dog. The focus was on learning proper form and getting comfortable with the movements.

After a few weeks, I gradually incorporated 5- to 8-lb dumbbells into the movements, and a month or two later, I noticed a real difference in my strength: I could do more repetitions, lift even heavier weights, and move with greater confidence. It was so encouraging to see the hard work pay off, and it motivated me to keep going. About a year into consistent training, I was feeling stronger and ready to take on more. I began training full-body twice a week and incorporated more challenging exercises like squat variations, the walking lunge, weighted glute bridge, and chest fly to build overall strength.

I’d never deadlifted before, so seeing someone my age lift with that kind of strength was incredibly inspiring. That decision marked the beginning of a new chapter in my strength training journey—I told my new trainer of about six months, Jack Tyree, that I wanted to lift heavier weights and try deadlifting. I even began training for my gym’s upcoming annual deadlift exhibition, which was in eight months.

Since I’d just been training with dumbbells, I tried working with a kettlebell while I got comfortable with the movement and proper technique. As I got stronger and more confident, I graduated to the barbell and continued adding more weight each week. Then, this past May, I deadlifted 132 lbs for a single rep at the exhibition, setting a personal record. I never imagined I’d be able to do something like that, but I was so proud of how strong I’d become—and I was excited to see how much further I could push myself.

Six months after the exhibition, I now strength train three days a week: one day focused on upper body, one on lower body, and one dedicated to mobility and balance. Jack still programs all my workouts, and every session includes six to eight exercises, with 3 or 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps each. I use a mix of free weights and weight machines, and some of my go-to moves include the farmer’s carry, curtsy lunge, lat pulldown, scapular pushup, squat, and bench press. Deadlifts are still my favorite; I can now do three reps at 132 lbs, which I’m really proud of.

Outside the gym, I love getting outside and staying active, so I walk a few miles with my dog every day for my cardiovascular health. In addition to mobility and balance work at the gym, I also try to stretch at home whenever I can to ease muscle soreness and improve my range of motion, especially in my shoulders and hips.

I know nutrition is an important part of recovery too. Although I don’t follow a strict nutrition plan or count macros, I try to eat protein at every meal to support muscle growth. Usually, it’s chicken, red meat, or a scoop of protein powder mixed into my morning oatmeal. I also prioritize whole foods and aim to incorporate a variety of fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

When I first started strength training, I didn’t know where to begin. So, having someone guide me through the movements, teach me proper form, and help me build strength safely made all the difference. My trainers have helped me recognize what I’m capable of, push beyond what I thought was possible, and progress at a pace that feels right. They also create workouts that challenge me while keeping my goals in mind. Having their support and encouragement has given me the confidence to try things I never imagined I could do. Whether it’s deadlifting heavy weights, bench pressing a barbell, or taking less rest between working sets, my trainers have taught me not to put a ceiling on what I think I can accomplish.

Before I strength trained, I felt weak and unsteady, but I didn’t give up and accept that I’d feel like that for the rest of my life. In some ways, I completely started over with exercise at 74 because I tried something brand new—and that’s affected my life outside of the gym.

Now, at 78, I feel stronger than ever; I can get up off the floor with ease, carry my own groceries into the house, shovel snow, garden, and play sports with my grandchildren. These are things I want to keep doing independently, and having the strength to do them confidently means the world to me. While I love lifting weights and hitting new PRs, the greatest reward is how much easier everyday life has become.

Learning to lift in my mid-70s wasn’t easy, and building that strength didn’t happen overnight, but I kept showing up, putting in the work, and gradually accomplishing what I once never thought was possible. Now, as I approach 80, I’m still getting stronger, and I want other women to know they’re never too old to get started, and they may be capable of far more than they realize. If I can go from struggling to get up from a curb to deadlifting 132 pounds, who knows what else is possible?

The new N8 EV, or “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza called it, is available in six variants, including four battery-electric (EV) and two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain options.

With BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, the Denza N8 EV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. Charging from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Like many of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is equipped with BYD’s premium tech and features, such as its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system and God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system.

#4637. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4636. A Complete Guide to Caring For Your Nails While Working Out

The gym: Great for muscle tone and cardiovascular health, less ideal for your nails. This advice will help keep your tips in top shape.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

THE ENDORPHINS, the physical changes you can see and feel in your body, the overall confidence boost that comes with doing something good for your body—yeah, the benefits of working out are hard to beat. The one area where a sweat session can fall short, however, is when it comes to the health of our nails.

If you're someone who loves a fresh manicure, especially one with some length, you know the struggle of keeping your tips intact at the gym. Between chipped polish, cracks and peeling, and the mental gymnastics of trying to avoid both, it can sometimes feel like your nails (and your sanity) are getting a workout of their own. “When I’m lifting plates or handling weights, I’m always conscious of how I’m gripping,” shares celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador Gina Edwards, who's a frequent gym-goer herself. “I use my finger pads rather than the tips of my fingers to help avoid putting unnecessary pressure on my nails.”

Meet the experts: Gina Edwards is a celebrity manicurist and KISS ambassador. Dana Stern, MD, is a New York-based dermatologist who specializes in nail disorders. Marisa Garshick, MD, is a dermatologist based in New York City. Jin Soon Choi is a celebrity manicurist in New York City.

Not into manicures? Unfortunately, that doesn't mean you're completely off the hook. Even bare nails can take a beating: “The nail is a thousand times more absorptive of water than the skin,” says New York dermatologist Dana Stern, MD, who specializes in nail disorders. And because frequent handwashing and exposure to moisture often go hand in hand with working out, nails are subjected to expansion as they absorb water and contraction as they dry. “Repeated wet-dry cycles can contribute to splitting and peeling, particularly in people already prone to brittle nails,” Dr Stern adds.

But not to worry—you don’t have to choose between having polished digits and getting your fitness on. With a few smart habits, you can avoid all the pitfalls. Here’s how.

No matter how you choose to work out, there are plenty of ways your nails can suffer. And most of us don't even realize we're putting them in harm's way until it's too late. Maybe you're in a workout class, engaging in some friendly competition with your neighbor to see who can knock out their burpees the fastest, only to jam a nail as your hands hit the ground. Or perhaps the damage happens before you even break a sweat. Picture it: You're pulling on your most compressive pair of leggings when a nail snags on the fabric or, worse, bends backward and breaks.

Of course, some activities pose a more obvious risk than others. Exercises that involve “repetitive gripping, pressure, or friction, such as weightlifting, rock climbing, and certain types of strength training” can be especially hard on your nails, says Marisa Garshick, MD, a dermatologist based in New York City.

Here are a few of the ways your workout routine might be doing a number on them:

Handling dumbbells, weight plates, and other equipment can put pressure on nails, especially if they're long, dry, or already weak, says celebrity manicurist Jin Soon Choi.

Jamming a nail against a hard surface or repeatedly putting pressure on it can cause the nail plate to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis. This can happen to natural nails, too, although extensions may create additional opportunities for snagging.

When a falsie gets caught on something, it can even cause the underlying natural nail to lift from the nail bed, explains Dr. Stern. Depending on the extent of the damage, it can take months for a healthy new nail to grow in.

Frequent handwashing and exposure to harsh cleansers (including those used to wipe down gym equipment and alcohol-based hand sanitizers) can contribute to splitting and peeling, Dr. Stern adds.

While running and cycling may be gentler on your hands, repeated pressure inside athletic shoes can cause bruising beneath the nail (known as a subungual hematoma), thickening, or even nail loss, explains Dr. Garshick.

The good news? Most workout-related nail damage is temporary, provided the nail matrix, which is responsible for nail growth, hasn't been damaged. But more serious injuries can have lasting consequences. A crush injury—heavy weight falling on a nail, for example—could cause permanent damage to the nail matrix, Dr. Stern says. Even when the damage isn't permanent, patience is key. According to Dr. Garshick, fingernails typically take three to six months to grow out, while toenails can take twelve to eighteen months.

The goal isn't to give up your favorite workouts or your favorite manicures. A few tweaks to your nail-care routine and how you handle equipment can make all the difference.

Here's what the pros recommend to keep your nails looking and feeling their best.

This ultra-nourishing product delivers a healthy dose of barrier-repairing ceramides, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide sans greasy residue.

Jinsoon Primrose + Honeysuckle Healing Cuticle Oil

Choi recommends this product, from her own line, before bed to help maintain healthy nails and cuticles.

You’ve heard of bond builders for hair, right? This is the same thing, but for nails. It promises longer, stronger nails in just four weeks.

It’s important to keep in mind that Dr. Garshick says not every nail change is workout-related. Persistent discoloration, thickening, or lifting can sometimes indicate a fungal infection, psoriasis, or another nail condition. A new or changing dark streak, particularly one that doesn't grow out, should also be evaluated by a board-certified dermatologist.

At the end of the day, you don't have to choose between crushing your fitness goals and keeping your nails in good shape. In fact, Choi points out that exercise itself can actually be beneficial for nail health, as physical activity promotes healthy circulation, helping deliver oxygen and nutrients to the tissues responsible for nail growth.

It's the accidental injuries and repeated pressure that can cause problems, not the workouts themselves. With a few simple adjustments to your nail-care routine and a bit more awareness of how you're handling equipment, you can keep breaking a sweat without breaking a nail.

#4635. How To Build Strength You’ll Actually Use In Daily Life, According To A Trainer

Strength training isn't just about what you can lift in the gym. It helps make everyday tasks easier, whether that's carrying heavy shopping bags and moving furniture or putting a suitcase in the overhead compartment on a flight.

As we get older, we naturally start to lose muscle mass, strength and bone density—at approximately 3-8% per decade after the age of 30—but regular strength training can help slow this down, reminds Andy Carr, trainer and head of fitness for Snap Fitness UK.

Thankfully, you don't need complicated exercises to see the benefits.

By focusing on simple, functional movements that mimic everyday activities, you can build strength that carries over into daily life and keeps you strong, active and confident as you get older.

“It's not necessary to spend hours lifting weights to build strength that makes a difference,” he explains. “Even two or three strength sessions a week can help, especially when you're focusing on compound exercises that work several muscle groups at once.”

Squats are one of the best exercises for building lower-body strength because—as a compound exercise—they work your thighs, glutes, and core all at once.

“These are the muscles you use when getting up from a chair, lifting something off the floor or crouching down to do some gardening,” says Carr. Keeping them strong can make a real difference to how easily you move around, particularly as you get older.

Step-ups are great for building leg strength and improving balance at the same time, says Carr.

“They're particularly useful for everyday activities like climbing stairs, walking uphill, or stepping onto curbs. As we age, maintaining strength and stability in our legs becomes increasingly important, and step-ups are a simple way to work on both,” he adds.

Farmer's carries are a brilliant exercise for building strength you actually use, because they're essentially the same movement as carrying heavy shopping bags.

“They work your grip, shoulders and core, helping you carry things more comfortably and with better stability. Grip strength can decline with age, so it's a really useful exercise to include in your routine,” says Carr.

Picking something up, whether it's a laundry basket, a suitcase or a bag of compost in the garden, involves your glutes, hamstrings, and back. Deadlifts strengthen all these muscles, explains Carr.

“They're a great way to build strength for everyday lifting, so those jobs feel easier and you're more confident handling heavier objects.”

Rows are ideal for strengthening your upper back and arms, which we use for pulling movements throughout the day, from opening heavy doors to pulling a garden hose across the lawn.

“They also help support good posture, particularly if you spend a lot of time sitting at a desk,” says Carr. “Using a resistance band makes it easy to adjust the difficulty as you get stronger.”

Incline push-ups are a great way to build upper-body strength, working your chest, shoulders, arms, and core.

“These muscles help with everyday pushing movements, whether that's moving a shopping cart, pushing open a heavy door, or getting yourself up from the floor,” says Carr.

They're also easy to adapt to your fitness level, so you can gradually increase the challenge as your strength improves.

We use rotational movements more than we probably realize, whether that's turning to put something in the back of the car, reaching across to pick something up or digging in the garden.

Woodchops are great for strengthening your core and improving your ability to twist and turn with control, Carr explains.

“That becomes particularly useful as we get older, helping us stay mobile and making everyday movements feel easier.”

#4630. How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s on every class schedule and all over your feed. So what does “sculpt” actually mean, and what can it do for you?

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

The exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” says Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

In the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, says physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

The term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” says Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”

In the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” says Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” says Ritchey.

If you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she says.

There's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she says. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own plans for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”

If you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

According to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” says Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

Ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she says. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”

It’s important to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

That’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”

In other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

What’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”

Ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

“It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey says. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

Beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”

Of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” says Girard.

So if you’ve been curious to try a new sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”

As the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most important ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” says Ritchey.

Have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The important thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” says Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

They can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she says. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”

Appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the New School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. Laura Girard, CPT, is a NASM-certified personal trainer, founder of The Energy Academy, and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Kristine Thomason is a writer and editor with over a decade of experience creating content for print and digital publications. Previously, she was the health and fitness director at mindbodygreen, and the fitness and wellness editor at Women’s Health. Kristine's work has appeared in Men's Health, Travel + Leisure, Health, and Refinery29, among others. She holds a journalism degree from New York University, and is certified in personal training by the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

#4629. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4627. SpaceX could announce $1.5 trillion Tesla merger in December: report

Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination. A deal could be announced as soon as December, which would make it the largest merger ever, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.

According to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved. December is the target, but early 2027 is also on the table.

One of the variables on the table is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. So, as expected, this is shaping up as SpaceX absorbing Tesla, not the other way around.

That fits the valuations. SpaceX is worth over $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, while Tesla sits around $1.5 trillion. For scale, the record for a single deal has long been Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000, and even SpaceX’s roughly $250 billion purchase of xAI (a private company at the time) earlier this year would be dwarfed.

Neither company commented. Tesla stock rose as much as 1.9% on the report.

We’ve been tracking this since May, when Musk first floated merging the two companies weeks before the SpaceX IPO. At the time, we called it the fourth time Musk would make a more than $1 billion self-dealing transaction, after SolarCity, Twitter/X, and Tesla’s $2 billion xAI investment that turned into SpaceX stock.

Then, in October, Tesla’s proxy filing read like a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has sat on SpaceX’s board since February. The ballot for the December 3 meeting is limited to re-electing Musk, chair Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to terms through 2029, plus a say-on-pay vote and the auditor.

A day later, Musk confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.

The governance piece is where Tesla shareholders should pay the most attention.

Musk owns about 20% of Tesla but controlled roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares, according to its S-1. Swapping Tesla shares for SpaceX shares means trading one-share-one-vote for a company where Musk’s control is effectively locked in.

And the deal itself pays Musk. Under the change-in-control terms in his 2025 CEO award, the operational milestones drop out and the market cap test runs at the deal price, with earned shares vesting immediately. Based on the share count in the proxy, a deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion (about a 33% premium to where it trades now) would clear the first market cap tranche on the spot. His 286 million restricted shares from the 2018 package also accelerate on a change in control.

Bloomberg reports that one of the main obstacles is how to ring-fence Tesla’s China business. A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s defense and government work and Tesla’s China footprint as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.

That’s the same issue behind the Wall Street Journal’s July report that Tesla was weighing a sale or spinoff of its China operations, which Musk denied. Giga Shanghai is Tesla’s most productive factory and builds more than half of its cars. It shipped 67,829 vehicles in October alone.

Politics is the other wild card. Congress flipped to Democrats in the midterms, and they’ve said Musk’s companies and his political ties will get a hard look. Bloomberg previously reported the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

I suspected that the midterms might accelerate the timeline. The Dems don’t take office until January, and Musk likely wants to move this as far along as possible before then.

No rational independent board would offer $1.5 trillion (much less $2 trillion) for Tesla. It is a shrinking EV company with a few fantasy projects that are not delivering. But endlessly diluting other stockholders is his thing.

As for the “independent committees”, those are obviously a joke. No one believes that, but it’s not like Tesla’s shareholders would care at this point. Tesla’s stock has been a dud for 4 years, and shareholders’ best chance to see a return is another self-deal with Musk.

Tesla is a car and energy company with falling car sales, and it would get folded into a rocket, satellite, and AI company that’s valued at a premium to it and controlled by one person.

This is the end game. At least, it looks like Elon is running out of companies to fold together to hide underperformance.

If you’re following Tesla because of its energy business, the cheapest way to tap into that transition at home is still putting solar on your own roof. #4626. Lunar’s new home DC fast charger puts your EV battery to work

Lunar Energy has unveiled a 25-kW home DC fast charger that will do more than just power up your car really fast. Paired with its next-generation home battery system, the Lunar Fast Charger will also let a compatible EV help keep the house running during an outage and potentially earn money by sending electricity back to the grid.

The new battery system will be available to customers in early 2027, with the charger rollout expected in mid-2027.

Lunar says its home DC fast charger can add roughly 100 miles of range in an hour at up to 25 kW. Actual results will depend on the vehicle and charging conditions.

This is a DC charger, according to Lunar’s product specifications. It connects directly to the DC side of the Lunar Battery, and Lunar says that setup avoids an electrical panel upgrade for the charger. The product page lists CCS and NACS connector support but doesn’t specify which cars will support bidirectional charging.

That distinction matters. Charging an EV and sending power back are separate capabilities, so buyers will need to check vehicle compatibility before relying on home backup.

With a compatible EV, Lunar says vehicle-to-home (V2H) charging could extend backup power through a multi-day outage. How long it lasts will depend on the car’s available battery capacity and what’s running in the house.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) payments will also depend on the availability of programs. They aren’t an automatic benefit of installing the charger.

The updated Lunar System has a 13.4 kW inverter and uses 5 kWh battery modules. A single tower holds 10–30 kWh, while towers installed side by side can provide up to 300 kWh.

Lunar is also expanding into small businesses, with pad-mounted configurations reaching 1 MWh. Businesses could use the batteries for backup and to reduce demand charges, or fees tied to their highest power draw.

The system can work with new solar using Lunar Maximizer panel optimizers, existing solar, or no solar at all. Lunar says assembly takes place in California, Georgia, Idaho, and Washington, with engineering and R&D in Mountain View, California.

Lunar AI uses electricity prices, weather forecasts, and a property’s energy use to decide when to charge batteries or supply power. Adding the EV gives it another battery to coordinate with rooftop solar and household battery storage.

The company reports that its California customers using Lunar AI saved an additional $338 on average last year compared with a standard battery operating mode.

Lunar’s Gridshare platform already manages more than 150,000 distributed energy devices worldwide. It groups those resources into virtual power plants (VPPs), allowing utilities and other energy providers to call on stored electricity when demand rises and offer customers incentives for participating. It currently operates VPPs in California, Hawaii, and Texas and is expanding in Utah, Nevada, and New Jersey. It also operates in Europe, the UK, and Japan.

Lunar hasn’t yet disclosed pricing or named compatible bidirectional EV models. Those are two important details homeowners will need before deciding whether this setup makes sense for their driveway.

#4625. Jennifer Lawrence’s Hair Care Brand Launch Faced Public Scrutiny—But How Do the Products Actually Perform?

I tested Mes° Beauty for two weeks to find out.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

When Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity. What we didn’t see coming was the launch of her new hair care brand Mes° Beauty (pronounced “mess”) and the public backlash that followed.

In an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public. “She saw the numbers Rihanna, Selena Gomez, and Hailey Bieber were pulling in, and suddenly decided to join Instagram, too. Not necessarily to connect with her audience, but perhaps to tap into the same commercial machine and sell us even more stuff,” wrote one Instagram commenter.

JLaw teamed up with Jasmina Aganovic, founder of biotech beauty company Arcaea Labs, to formulate the brand’s hair care. As they say, the proof is in the pudding, so when I was sent all three products in a PR mailer, I knew I wanted to put them to the test.

Read my full, honest review of Mes° Beauty’s hair mask, serum, and volume mist below.

An intensive repair mask designed to be applied to dry hair anytime before washing. The milky-colored mask has a silky yet sticky, gelatin-like consistency that clings to your hair as you apply it. According to the brand, the mask prevents breakage and wash-day protein loss and protects the hair’s lipid barrier.

The Multitask Repair Mask differs from other hair masks because you apply it before shampooing and can leave it on for five minutes or overnight. With such a wide treatment time, it might take some trial and error to find the “sweet spot” for your hair type. During my testing, I applied a generous coat of the mask 5 to 10 minutes before shampooing. The second time, I tried applying a thinner coat of the mask, then pinned my hair up with a claw clip for about two hours before rinsing it out. The longer you wear it, the better the results. I would recommend applying a light coat before going about your day; that way, the scent isn’t overpowering and it won’t drip on your clothes.

After just two uses, my hair looked shinier and felt more hydrated after styling. As someone who rarely plans my hair care routine ahead of time, I appreciate that I can apply the mask just five minutes before I hop in the shower and still get noticeable results.

Although Mes° says the mask doubles as a styler for a glossy wet-hair look, I wouldn’t use it in that way. I think the product's consistency is too sticky and would be uncomfortable and messy (literally) to wear all day.

Some reviewers have mentioned a slightly off-putting smell. While the scent doesn’t bother me (it smells like a light, musky fragrance), it may not be for everyone. If I’m paying $52 for a hair mask, it would be nice to have a luxurious fragrance to add to the experience. If a brand is going to do musk, really lean into it with notes of sandalwood, amber, or patchouli.

The packaging also makes the product difficult to use. In the mailer I received, the mask comes in a GoGo Squeez-like pouch that you’re supposed to empty into the plastic tub. However, dipping my fingers into the tub felt clumsy, and next time I would just dispense directly from the pouch.

A bi-phase serum that smooths frizz, restores shine, and provides heat protection up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The “bi-phase” claim comes from combining a lightweight oil and a serum in the formula. After touching it, applying it, and letting it sit in my hair for a few days, I think calling it a serum is misleading. The consistency and the way it applies are much more like a hair oil.

On day two hair, I warmed two drops of the Off-Duty Restyling Serum between my palms, and worked it through my strands. I have very thick, straight, shoulder-length hair, so when I applied the serum up through my mid-lengths, it was way too oily. I don’t know if I would use it to restyle my hair unless I was planning to use a hot tool.

I also tested the serum as a finishing product, applying it to my ends after blow-drying. I found this to be the most effective way to use the product on my hair type.

Overall, the Off-Duty Restyling Serum doesn’t make much sense to me. What’s the point of having heat protection if it’s made for “reshaping yesterday’s style?” Are we going back in with more heat? To me, that sounds like an extra step in my morning routine that I do not have the time or patience for.

On days when I wash and blow-dry my hair, I like using a tiny amount of the serum just on my ends, and I've found it dries down nicely and leaves my hair soft and touchable. That said, I own other lightweight hair oils that work just as well for a fraction of the price—like FromLabs’ Protein Capsule Hair Repair Oil. If you have fine, wavy, or curly hair, the Off-Duty Serum may work better for you.

A lightweight spray that reduces scalp oiliness for lasting lift. Instead of creating gritty texture or absorbing excess oil like a dry shampoo, the Good Roots mist helps balance the scalp microbiome to produce less oil at the roots, extending the time until your next wash.

Over the past two weeks, I tested the Good Roots mist in three ways: applying it to damp hair before blow-drying, applying it to damp hair before air-drying, and applying it to dry day-two and day-three hair.

After about five uses of trial and error, I found it worked best when I applied it to my clean, damp roots and blow-dried. The heat felt like it helped dry down and “activate” the mist, whereas letting my hair air-dry didn’t produce much volume.

Pro-Tip: Be sure to hold the bottle about a foot away for even misting. The applicator pump doesn’t produce a fine spritz, and it took me a few uses to get that right.

After two weeks of testing, the Good Roots Volume Mist is my favorite of the trio. Two key ingredients, the proprietary Arc-5 Technology and the Mediterranean microalgae, help support a balanced scalp, keeping your hair fresher longer. With consistent use, the Good Roots mist extended my time between hair washes—I typically wash every other day, but I was able to go a third day. Plus, the Juniperus virginiana oil in the formula has a fresh, woody scent that reminds me of a fancy sea salt spray.

I also like that the mist doesn’t make my hair feel super gritty or textured the way a dry shampoo might. That said, I have other dry shampoo products that do a lot more heavy lifting than this volume mist. If I’m looking to achieve noticeable volume and lift in my thick hair, the Good Roots mist doesn’t cut it.

My general critique of Mes° Beauty is that the products are not very intuitive. They seem straightforward, but the brand doesn’t give great direction on how to get the most out of them. After the first one or two uses, you may feel they barely do anything at all. But if you learn how to use them properly when styling your hair, they can perform fairly well.

Mes° is supposed to be about “Less time fixing your hair. More time living,” but in reality, achieving that effortlessly chic, tousled look requires a fair bit of effort. In my opinion, this lineup is much more suited to someone who blows out or flat irons or curls their hair once or twice a week and wants to extend their style. For my hair type, these products don’t fit into my routine in a way that makes sense, but if you have fine and/or wavy hair, they might work better for you.

Curious about my other hair standbys? They’re currently $30 and under—and make for excellent beauty gift ideas for your loved ones for the upcoming holiday season.
