#4584. Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 new cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she said.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang said those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang said that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang said she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The New England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen said.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang said she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”

#4583. Why Feeling Good Is Good for You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Identifying small wins and feeling proud of ourselves releases dopamine and oxytocin (feel-good chemicals), wiring the brain to build lasting self-worth. This motivates us to seek out more of those moments to optimize our lives and be happier. Naturally, evolutionary selection favors traits that help us thrive and perpetuate the species.

That’s why examples of human greatness in many different artistic mediums and professional fields move us so much. It’s natural for people to consciously or unconsciously desire a small piece of relative immortality. However, not necessarily the kind of lofty immortality of performing miracles, finding the cure for cancer, or winning championships as a professional athlete. I actually mean finding ways to discover a sense of pride and purpose in what we do, every day, whether it’s in our jobs, how we raise our families, how we treat others, etc. We all want to feel the same excellence that we sometimes admire in our fellow humans. We all want to leave a legacy, a footprint, before we “shuffle off this mortal coil.”

When I was in my mid-30s, I became frustrated with my less-than-adequate golf game. Golf is not a simple sport to learn. It can be maddening to grasp even the fundamental mechanics of a golf swing. Author Harry Leon Wilson wrote that “golf has too much walking to be a good game, and just enough game to spoil a good walk.”

But I was lucky enough to have found a unique golf instructor named Allen at one of the Los Angeles public golf courses. His method of teaching stuck with me. It not only helped improve my game but it boosted my confidence and even my self-esteem. Allen was not just a golf instructor; he was a motivator and an amateur philosopher.

During the first lesson, Allen observed me hit countless golf balls at the driving range. He offered me zero verbal feedback. He just watched. The next time we met, he videotaped approximately 50 of my swings from the golf tee. Of those 50 swings, I only hit the ball correctly about five times. In other words, 90% of the time, I hit the ball incorrectly. But that was not important to him. He was more interested in the 10% of times I did hit the ball correctly.

That week, he edited the video by discarding the 45 bad swings and only keeping the five correct swings. For the next three or four sessions, we began the lesson by watching a video loop of the five correct swings over and over again. As we watched, he specifically pointed out everything I was doing right. He highlighted every tiny detail of positivity in my swing with great enthusiasm. The point being that he was less concerned in telling me what I was doing incorrectly and more interested in what I was doing correctly. Keep in mind, the edited loop with the five good swings was less than 30 seconds, but its impact was infinite. Suddenly my imagined inadequacy became abstract.

Over the next few months, the more I watched the edited video of the correct swings, the more I felt pleased about my golf game. I also noticed a renewed sense of self-assurance. Allen was obviously using basic positive reinforcement to boost my confidence and to teach me better golf mechanics, but what it also did was inspire me to be better, not only at playing golf, but at other things too. Allen stirred me to wonder what else I was capable of achieving. I became impressed by my own potential, and by tapping into this sense of personal achievement, I didn't just become a better golfer, I was also stimulated to improve every area of my life.

Do you sometimes see yourself as inadequate because you're not an expert at something? Or you feel “less than,” because you haven’t accomplished amazing things in your life? Do you believe that the allegedly talented people in the world are just born with natural gifts? Do you think you have to be a genius to succeed? If so, you are missing out on creating the kind of intention you need to feel good about yourself. Hence, the positive affirmation exposure I experienced with my golf instructor Allen is something we need to practice alone. But the goal is not about being great or needing to be a genius at something.

According to research, there is much more to the notion of a born genius. For example, some people may be born with, let’s say, an inclination toward art and music, math and sciences, business and finance, or even sports and athletics. But to master that inclination, you need years of preparation and practice. Author Malcolm Gladwell tells us it takes approximately 10,000 hours of practice to become an expert in any field. So, genius is not something that is necessarily born, but rather created through deliberate training, repetition, and rehearsal. Genius is perseverance in disguise. It’s learning how to give yourself encouragement one small win at a time. That’s why feeling good about you, is good for you.

So, when we—as theoretically typical human beings—are exposed to greatness and achievement (our own or others'), we are filled with appreciation of what is possible in our lives too. Giving ourselves positive affirmations lifts our spirits even when we are feeling low, depressed, or anxious.

Let’s also remember that we don't need to be better than others to feel secure. Evolution didn't design us to carry the weight of the universe. Instead, it asks only that we show up and do the small things with purpose.

By embracing this, we unlock an innate capacity for healing and personal growth. In the end, greatness isn't something reserved exclusively for others; it's a mirror reflecting the boundless potential waiting to be awakened within us all.

Gladwell, M. (2005). Blink: The power of thinking without thinking. Little, Brown and Company.

Wilson, H. L. (1905). The Boss of Little Arcady. Lothrop, Lee & Shepard Co.

Magsamen, S., & Ross, I. (2023). Your brain on art: How the arts transform us. Canongate Books.

Shakespeare, W. (2008). Hamlet. In S. Greenblatt (Ed.), The Norton Shakespeare (2nd ed., pp. 1659–1759). W. W. Norton & Company. (Original work published 1603)

#4582. Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Whether cartridge or electric, these provide the smoothest, most comfortable shave.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

LIKE MOST SCRUFFY men, I’ve had a complicated relationship with razors. Why risk razor burn or slicing your neck for something that’s going to grow back in two days? But I’ve come to realize it’s the same reason you wear pants even though you have to clean them after. Because you don’t want to look disheveled (or denied access to restaurants). Plus, with the right technique and grooming products, one razor can give you the closest, most gentle shave possible.

Now that you’re on board with razors, it’s time to find the right tool for you. People constantly debate the best shaving method—some claim more blades give a better shave, while others argue they cause more irritation and ingrown hairs to sensitive skin. Some dudes ride for high-tech electric razors, others stand by their old-school safety razors.

As board-certified dermatologist Dr. Azadeh Shirazi, MD, puts it, there is no right or wrong answer. It comes down to personal preference and need. These are the best options for every skin type and budget.

Razors do not get better than Gillette's Fusion5—it’s a classic for a reason. According to celebrity hairstylist and master barber Cody Renegar, the blades are flexible enough to maintain contact with your skin at all times, while an added conditioning pad helps them glide over the skin without lifting or creating cuts. Plus, the stretchy microfin design, featuring soft and flexible horizontal fins that help stretch skin before the blades make contact, ensures a close and smooth shave.

The built-in precision trimmer, a single-edged blade positioned on the backside of the razor cartridge, also brings about a cleanly sculpted shave. This extra single blade on the top edge creates sharp detailing (like around the sideburns or mustache) without digging into your skin. Not to mention, this razor is one of the more affordable options on the market (under $6 a blade), and refills are widely available at any drugstore.

When it comes to shaving, more blades aren’t always better, but in the case of this razor, five is the lucky number. These cartridges pack in the shaving power with five blades and a larger lubrication strip, the combo of which delivers a smoother, closer shave without as much irritation.

These blades last about five shaves (one for each blade), which is a pretty good deal when compared with other, lower-priced blades that get dull faster. The handle itself is lightweight and easy to hold, with a rubberized feel that works well in the shower if you’re that kind of shaver.

Pamper yourself with a hot towel shave using Gillette's Heated Razor. It transforms a barbershop-style shave into an at-home experience, warming the blades with chargeable, heating cartridges that soften hair as you shave.

Its stainless steel warming bar and flexible five-blade design work together to deliver a more comfortable, closer shave. The waterproof razor features an adjustable heat setting, letting you find your perfect temperature. Plus, it comes with a handy rechargeable stand.

It’s usually best to approach gadgets like this with a healthy dose of skepticism, and honestly, many of them don't live up to their promises. But this heated razor is one of the exceptions. In fact, it exceeds expectations. The stainless steel bar heats up to various temperatures depending on your comfort level (don’t worry, even the highest setting won’t burn your skin).

The combination of heat and five blades delivers a noticeably closer, more comfortable shave. The overall experience is smoother, and I noticed less irritation and razor burn than I usually get with non-heated razors. To be clear, at over $100 for the kit ($200 with the case), this is a luxury razor kit. But the futuristic heated design and ultra-smooth shave make it a worthwhile investment, if you can swing the price tag.

Read More: Gillette Labs Heated Razor Review

An electric razor that doesn’t pull or irritate your skin, even during the adjustment period? Yes, please. I’ve been boasting about the 100 percent waterproof Braun Series 9 Pro for years.

The built-in AutoSense technology, which reads the thickness of your facial hair and automatically adjusts the power of the shaver's motor accordingly, provides a customized shave, and the ten-direction flex head makes sure to get every single spot with titanium-coated blades. Really, this is the Ferrari of razors right here—hence the price tag.

In my extensive testing of electric razors, this one stood out head and shoulders above the rest due to its tech-packed design that actually does deliver a more efficient shave, even if you have days' worth of stubble.

It effectively cuts shaving time in half, and you’re able to use it both wet and dry (with or without shaving cream). However you choose to use it, if you’re thinking of making the switch to an electric shave, this is the best possible option.

This innovative electric razor shaves smoothly, cleanly, and efficiently without nicking or cutting—you can easily rub it back and forth on the skin—with long-lasting replaceable blades. While it won’t get you as close a shave as the other options on this list, it will give you a low stubble that makes you look rugged yet refined.

In fact, Dr. Penzi says that it’s the most reliable electric shaver for men prone to ingrown hairs who don’t mind maintaining some stubble. The real beauty of this electric razor-trimmer hybrid, however, is that you can use it for literally any look, anywhere you want to shave. It gives a close, clean shave on both your face and body, but also comes with length guards if you want to keep some length.

The OneBlade will always be a winner because it’s so easy to use. Built like a classic razor, but with the power of an electric shave, the best thing about this device is the innovative blade, which delivers a close, fast shave with very little risk of nicking or cutting. The multiple guards allow you to customize the length of your shave.

Plus, it’s waterproof and can be used in the shower. It’s also just as effective on your body as on your face, making it an indispensable tool for all your shaving needs. Just be sure to switch the blade when using it on your body to cut down on the risk of cross-contamination of bacteria.

Read More: Philips Norelco OneBlade Review

It’s hard to beat the price of this simple yet effective razor. Dr. Garshick loves that it’s a travel-friendly razor that’s gentle on skin. It uses a soothing, lubricated strip containing aloe vera to calm the skin while giving you a close, smooth shave anywhere you use it. Best of all is the fact that you get a total of eight cartridges in this pack, making it the best value on this list.

Disposable razors are great for certain scenarios, like travel, but they can also be pretty wasteful and, worse, not very effective. But the five-blade cartridges of this razor are equally as effective as a reusable razor with a similar design, so you’re not compromising on efficacy when choosing a disposable razor.

That being said, compared to other razors on this list, the blades will get dull quickly (after a few uses), but that’s pretty standard for a disposable.

According to Dr. Shirazi, this is the perfect safety razor: It's weighted for better control, comes with a single blade to counter ingrown hairs and irritation, and has high-quality blades for a smooth shave with each stroke. Dr. Garshick also approves of Bevel's single, double-edged blade, which she notes helps to achieve a close shave without needing to apply a lot of pressure.

Of course, it takes a village to help limit the chances of ingrown hair and take down facial hair, so this kit has everything you need. It includes gentle shave cream, relieving post-shave balm, and 40 (!) blade refills.

There is a learning curve when switching from a cartridge razor to a safety razor, so the first few times you use this razor, it’s going to take longer than you’re used to. But once you get the hang of it, including the all-important 30-degree angle, it does go faster. Though you don’t want to go too fast, as it’s easy to nick or cut yourself with this sharp, single blade.

It delivers a close shave, cutting down on the amount of ingrown hairs and post-shave irritation, which is why many people switch to a safety razor to begin with. The handle is perfectly weighted to feel hefty in your hand but still glide smoothly across your skin, making the actual act of shaving a pleasure.

If you have sensitive skin or are prone to irritation, shaving can become a unique form of torture. Gillette, however, has a solution. According to Dr. Shirazi, its SkinGuard razor comes with a special guard on the blade that prevents it from shaving too close but doesn’t sacrifice efficacy. It cushions every movement, eliminating tugging and helping sensitive skin stay soothed and comfortable, she says.

While the two-blade design won't provide a baby-smooth shave, you can still get a pretty close cut without the rash. Besides the ease of use, Dr. Garshick also highlights the comfort of its added lubrication for an easy glide, as well as its precision trimmer for hard-to-reach areas.

When you have sensitive skin, too many blades can destroy your face. This razor, however, just comes with two blades, plus a Skinguard feature that helps minimize how much the blades drag over your skin. The less close shave is a compromise, for sure, but it really does help protect sensitive skin from post-shave irritation. The blades are spaced out to help prevent nicks and tugs, as well—a design feature that resulted in zero (!) irritation or cuts with my first use.

In general, razors with more blades deliver a closer shave, but they also come with drawbacks. Additional blades will provide a closer and quicker shave; however, an increased risk of irritation and ingrown hairs is the tradeoff. Razors with only one or two blades are much gentler on skin, but don’t cover as much at once.

These deliver a closer shave than most razors—even with just one blade—thanks to their sharp edge. That being said, these are also the most dangerous. With the wrong technique, you’re more likely to get cuts than with any other razor type.

The most common razor you’ll find in any grooming aisle. Blade design plays the biggest role here—whether you use more blades or fewer. But compared to safety razors, these won’t get as close, but the risk of serious skin slicing is much lower.

Electric razors won’t give you as close a shave as blades because their heads don’t make full contact with the skin. However, they still shave close enough to keep stubble low, neat, and often unnoticeable. Dermatologist Dr. Lauren Penzi, MD, recommends electric razors for people prone to ingrown hairs since they cut hair above the skin’s surface.

According to dermatologist Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD, it’s important to consider the blade count, as multi-blade razors offer a closer shave, but a higher risk of irritation. While many go for a five-blade design because it'll shave faster and closer than a two-blade or one-blade (fewer strokes are needed), Dr. Shirazi argues that this can be overkill and more dangerous.

He warns that more blades can often lead to more friction and thus irritation, so it’s best to use fewer blades (no more than two) to reduce your risk of razor bumps and irritation if you have sensitive skin.

That’s not to say a single-blade design can’t also provide a close shave, if you know the right technique. If you’re prone to irritation or ingrown hairs, dermatologist Dr. Brendan Camp, MD, agrees on using razors with a single or double blade. For men with coarser, thicker hair, Dr. Penzi suggests multi-blade razors, which often deliver a closer, smoother cut with fewer strokes—reducing friction and irritation. In short, for the closest shave, go above three blades. For the gentlest shave, aim for below that number.

Every razor comes with its own features and strengths, because getting a clean shave is only half the battle. Before you buy, look for specs that make shaving easier and more comfortable, like handle design, waterproofing, cleaning docks, or built-in trimmers.

After a few hundred strokes, or five to seven shaves, blades become dull. That said, when you're buying reusable razors, you should opt for one that has easy-to-replace refills to achieve a smooth and close shave every time. You’ll want to keep an eye on how many blades are included in the initial pack, as this will cut down on cost and how soon you’ll have to re-up after buying.

We've been testing every type of razor since this article was first published in 2018. For this update, I teamed up with fellow Men's Health editors and writers over the past year to identify which razors are currently the best-performing. Drawing from years of testing feedback and my own experience as a grooming editor and overall hairy dude, I narrowed the list down to 25 razors to trial or reevaluate. I also spoke with other grooming experts, including professional barbers and board-certified dermatologists, on which razors they recommend.

We then judged each one for effectiveness, price, ease of use, and long-term performance, as well as how frequently they caused irritation. After this research and weeks of testing each product, I landed on the seven options above as the best razors for men in 2026.

No matter what razor you use, always make sure it’s sharp (switch it after a few uses) since a dull razor will wreak havoc on your face. The most important thing is making sure the blade isn’t dull, as that can increase the potential for ingrowns and irritation, says Dr. Garshick.

It’s crucial to start by wetting your face with warm water to soften facial hair, says celebrity barber Ray Santos. "When I have time, I like to apply a hot towel directly to my skin for a few minutes before the shave to really prep my face."

Lathering up your face with cooling shaving gel will help protect the skin from irritation. Apply it evenly over the area you plan to shave to help the blades glide smoothly across your skin, Santos says.

To help prevent irritation, follow the natural direction that your facial hair grows when shaving. Keep in mind that hair doesn’t grow uniformly—what works for your cheeks might not apply to your neck or jawline, so pay attention to the grain in each area.

This includes not shaving too fast or pulling your skin taut while shaving, which will tighten the skin and give you a closer shave. But Dr. Camp warns of the latter technique's risk of razor bumps. And always shave after a shower or using a face wash when facial hair is at its softest and easiest to cut.

#4580. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4579. Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Learn the basics to keeping your heart healthy

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

Compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

“Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

“Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”

Chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he said that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”

An AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

“Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

“Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”

Other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen said.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

“Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen said.

“Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

Still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”

#4578. UFOs Are a Scientific Problem

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Last week, I had an argument with a friend that went like this: "UFOs are real." "No, they're not." "Yes, they are." "No, they're not."

You get the idea. There's a lot about philosophy of language, as a subdiscipline of philosophy, that is beyond me. But my one important takeaway from struggling through that class in graduate school was this: People will forever argue at cross-purposes if they don't first define their terms.

When considering the question of whether UFOs are real or not, we should be careful not to fall into the trap—a long-standing American tradition—of conflating UFOs with aliens. People still, in 2026, cringe when someone brings up the subject of UFOs because the conversation inevitably devolves into clichés about little green men and alien abductions. But "UFO" of course doesn't stand for "alien"; it stands for "unidentified flying object," which could turn out to be anything from a bird to a plane to Superman.

When did this conflation originate? Likely in the mid-20th century when UFO sightings spiked and pop culture was flooded with sci-fi tropes of flying saucers and aliens. But the misunderstanding lives on: Just the other day I overheard a professor ask a college student if she believed in UFOs. The student, an astrophysics major, laughed and said "No." I'd argue both the question and the answer are confused.

Ask yourself: Does it make sense to say that one doesn't believe in unidentified flying objects? This claim means you don't think it's possible that someone could look up in the sky and see something they can't identify. But this claim seems absurd. What UFOs are, and whether aliens from outer space visit us here on Earth, are two distinct questions and should be treated as such.

Putting aside the alien question, if our claim is simply that people do indeed see things the sky that they're unable to identify, then our astrophysics major would have to agree. The field of astrophysics wouldn't have come into being without people who studied the night sky and discovered things they couldn't identify and didn't understand.

Two 21st-century trends have brought the reality of UFOs into the light: 1) the internet has made it easier for both expert (e.g., airplane pilots) and non-expert UFO experiencers to share their stories, which helped legitimize UFO sightings as a shared and more common human experience than previously thought ; and 2) the Congressional hearings (begun in 2022) wherein trained military pilots shared their stories publicly lent further legitimacy to the phenomena as real, fascinating, and worthy of scientific study.

People see weird stuff in our skies all the time and in the vast majority of sightings, experts agree, these objects are ultimately identified as natural phenomena—lightning, satellites, lenticular clouds, airplanes, etc. But a small percentage of these sightings remain unidentified because they don't fit into our familiar classifications of reality with regard to how they look or behave, or both.

Jacques Vallee, a mathematician and astronomer who's authored dozens of books on UFOs, is one scientist who's always taken the UFO question seriously. He points out in his 1965 book, Anatomy of a Phenomenon, this ironic observation: Scientists are rational, analytical, and data-driven, until it comes to UFOs. Then they're emotional, gut-reactive, and dismissive of the data, which in ufology (so far) comes mainly in the form of first-person accounts. He notes that scientists have traditionally been content to wait for radio signals from outer space as evidence of extraterrestial intelligence (which assumes other forms of life traffic in radio signals) rather than collecting data on the innummerable acounts of UFO encounters from credible earthlings.

We don't yet know what UFOs are or where they're from though there are some hypotheses (in order from more familiar to least familiar): 1) they're (human-made) secret military vehicles either domestic or foreign; 2) they're humanoids from other dimensions of spacetime; 3) they're objects from lesser known regions on earth like the deep ocean depths; 4) they're visitors from other parts of the galaxy; and 5) they're mirages, holograms, or ephemeral elements of the universe's consciousness.

Science usually begins with wanting to understand something that is unknown. But in the case of UFOs, it might require a paradigm shift in thought from a deep-seated denial about intelligence in the universe to an acceptance that this indeed seems to be true. In Vallee's words, "They cannot replace in their imaginations the huge cosmic cemetery for celestial bodies which they describe in their books with a world of life and thought" (Vallee, 1965).

Vallée, J. (1965). Anatomy of a phenomenon: Unidentified objects in space—A scientific appraisal. Henry Regnery Company.

#4577. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4576. The 7 Best LED Face Masks for Men in 2026, According to Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

For battling blemishes and signs of aging, there are few better at-home tools.

AS SOMEONE RAISED on slasher horror movies, I was always going to gravitate towards LED face masks. But while their creepy Jason Voorhees-at-a-rave look is what initially grabbed my attention, the skincare benefits are what sold me on the products. LED face masks combine the firming power of anti-aging products, the depuffing of eye cream, the energizing boost of moisturizers, and the breakout-fighting strength of acne washes—making them one of the most versatile grooming tools out there.

LED masks use specific wavelengths of light to penetrate the skin and trigger cellular changes, according to dermatologist Dr. Hannah Kopelman, MD. This can include stimulating collagen production to reduce fine lines and support firmer skin, as well as treating acne-causing bacteria and calming inflammation to promote a clearer complexion. Some devices offer all of these benefits, while others are laser-focused (get it?) on just one or two. The key is to know what each is capable of and what service you’re looking for.

Dermatologist Dr. Brian Toy, MD, warns that the market is flooded with LED face masks that vary greatly in quality and effectiveness, so it’s best to start your search as informed as possible. To temper the confusion, I went ahead and used myself, along with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors, as guinea pigs. This way, you’ll know what works and what is merely an overpriced Halloween mask.

We gave Shark Beauty CryoGlow a 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award barely a month after it was released; that’s how great this LED mask is. It offers four separate treatment options that cover anything you could possibly want out of an LED face mask. The Better Aging setting uses red and infrared light to reduce wrinkles and firm skin, while Skin Clearing mode combines blue, red, and infrared light to fight blemishes and even tone.

The Skin Sustain maintains glow with a quick mix of all three LED wavelengths, and Under-Eye Revive uses cryotherapy-inspired cooling to depuff and tighten the under-eye area. You can also use this under-eye cooling ability combined with the other treatments, which roll out in three increasing levels of chill. Each is between four and eight minutes, meaning you don’t need to dedicate much time to combat whatever issue you’re after. Under-Eye Revive, you can do up to 15 minutes if you’d like, but you only need five to be effective.

Dr. Peterson Pierre, MD, FAAD, likes that this device uses red, blue, and infrared lights so that you can get a full smorgasbord of benefits, like combating acne, fighting signs of aging, reducing inflammation, and helping regulate oil production. He also digs the cooling feature and three levels of intensity. I’ve been using my CryoGlow for months, and have seen a noticeable change in the smoothness and clearness of my skin, as well as reduced redness, using The Better Aging and Skin Clearing settings. But where I saw the most immediate results was with eye puffiness.

If I’m ever running on limited sleep or recovering from a night out, I pop the mask on, and after a few minutes of Under-Eye Revive mode, I look like I’ve actually slept. The light from this device doesn’t feel glaring when you’re wearing it, so I was able to successfully walk around and multitask during my treatments.

Plus, as someone who is generally sensitive to light, it also feels a lot less intense than other options on this list, and never inspired headaches of any kind. Not to mention, it’s easy to adjust and fits my face perfectly. I only have a few nitpicks. Given the expansive options and customizability of this mask, there is a handheld controller attached to it to help you navigate. While this makes firing up the device super easy and you don’t need to rely on an app, the controller can be a bit awkward to deal with while you’re in treatment.

You can’t put it in your pocket without accidentally changing the setting, so you have to hold it, which limits the multitasking you’re able to do. Also, the mask is bulkier than its main competition for best overall, the Dr. Dennis Gross Face Mask. But when you consider that the CryoGlow is also the cheapest full-face option on this list, it’s a fair trade-off.

Dr. Kopelman has been recommending this LED mask to patients for years. She likes that it is FDA-cleared and offers both red and blue light; however, what she likes most about it is that it consistently delivers results. In terms of effectiveness, it’s equal to the CryoGlow. The only reason it just missed out on the top spot is that it’s over $100 more expensive and offers fewer additional treatments, like under-eye cooling. Beyond that, I find it just as successful at battling blemishes and signs of aging as the Shark Beauty.

Plus, the treatments are shorter, and you only need to wear this for three minutes a day to see results. Unlike many other options, like the CurrentBody or FAQ 202, which are made of more flexible material you can mold to your face, this design is rigid. While that may seem like a drawback, I loved it. Of all the LED masks on this list, I found Dr. Dennis Gross to be the sturdiest, and it fit my face perfectly. It’s slim, without feeling flimsy, and doesn’t weigh down my face like other similarly sturdy masks that tend to be a bit heavier, such as the Theraface Mask.

That being said, I possess an incredibly average build and face shape, so if you fall outside of those parameters, the singular and unadaptable design of this mask might not be as perfect a fit. Unlike the CryoGlow, it’s wireless when you’re using it and can be conveniently charged with any USB-C charger. This helps when traveling, though the solid design poses some challenges if you’re tight on storage space.

Similar to the Dr. Dennis Gross mask, this device is crafted with a hard, contoured shell; however, it’s far less slim. But it trades off this added bulkiness with its vibrating ability, which soothes facial tension and boosts blood flow around the eyes, brows, and scalp. It offers red, blue, and infrared light therapy to target acne, improve skin tone, and increase collagen production.

You can choose between three- or nine-minute treatment modes, though we found the longer sessions to be more effective. Sure, this mask can feel a bit heavy or bulky on the face, but the results are legit. In fact, some effects can be seen immediately, and they only increase from there. “After the very first time I used it, my skin felt softer, and my pores looked smaller,” says Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower.

“Over time, my skin tone looks more even, and my skin appears to be firmer, smoother, and less puffy.” He adds that the massaging, vibrating feature is relaxing, although it can feel ticklish or even chill-inducing at times. Since it sits close to your ears, it can also get a bit loud, especially when multitasking. Still, it’s really easy to switch between settings, turn on and off, and choose the massage style you want.

If you’re solely looking to combat puffiness, dark circles, and wrinkles, Lumin is the way to go. Sure, it looks straight out of an abandoned Lone Ranger In Space reboot, but there is no device better at rejuvenating the skin around the eyes than this mask. One tester saw noticeable improvements after days of use with this device. “I naturally have darker circles, but after consistent daily use for about a week, I saw a noticeable difference in the brightness and overall alertness of my eye area,” she says. The mask stays in place well, and the soft silicone padding makes it comfortable throughout each session.

Its adjustable design also ensures it fits all face shapes and sizes with ease. The same tester also saw a brighter tone and smoother skin after a couple of weeks of daily use. “While I don’t personally have under-eye wrinkles, I can see how this would be especially helpful for someone who does or for anyone who spends a lot of time in the sun,” she says. Not to mention, the Luminator is quick and easy to use—just three minutes a day with an auto timer.

Once the app is set up and the mask is synced, navigating the features becomes straightforward—just select your desired treatment and that’s it. Despite being covered in tiny LED lights, the mask feels surprisingly lightweight and comfortable. During the 15-minute session, testers reported no heat or noticeable sensation on the skin and even forgot it was on while doing other tasks, such as reading. The mask stays comfortably in place, even when looking down at a book or phone.

We also appreciated the included cleaning spray. For anyone with sensitive or breakout-prone skin, keeping the mask clean is essential, and the spray makes that simple. After each use, we cleaned and dried the mask before placing it in its pouch, which securely holds the device and makes storage hassle-free. One minor concern was the split at the bridge of the nose—designed for flexibility—which left one tester wondering if that area was receiving full treatment. Still, this didn’t deter them from continuing to use it.

Women’s Health fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says that the Qure Pro LED Mask has taken her nightly skincare regimen to the next level. After a month of use, she saw a dramatic difference in her skin’s appearance. She used to struggle with oily skin and frequent breakouts, but since regularly using the pink LED light setting, she says it has significantly reduced her sebum production. “I'm also approaching 30 (yikes), so I've been using the red LED light setting as well to help combat fine lines and reverse skin aging,” Accardi says.

Each session runs for three minutes and automatically shuts off when it’s done, so you never have to worry about timing it yourself. It’s perfect for anyone who wants results without the hassle. It’s one of the easiest, most low-maintenance skincare tools out there at a relatively low cost. That’s not to say $380 is cheap, but when it comes to legit, effective LED masks, you won’t find many other options under $400. It’s really just this and the CryoGlow.

If the more rigid masks, like CryoGlow, Qure, and Dr. Dennis Gross, are too bulky for you, but the FAQ is too small for your face, Currentbody will be your best option. This mask offers the most flexibility, with a silicone design that easily molds to the contours of any face, ensuring full coverage. This is as long as you tighten the straps. I’ve been lazy a few times with that, and it will start slipping off your face mid-treatment. In addition to the flexible fit, this mask feels super gentle on the face.

One of our testers used it only days after getting eye surgery with no issue. Didn’t bother her eyes one bit. That being said, it takes up to six hours for a full charge, which can be a bit annoying. This is the longest charge time on this list by a few hours, to be clear. I’m the type of person who pushes off charging a device until I absolutely have to, so this long charge time usually results in me skipping a day of treatment. But if you’re a better planner (to be fair, it’s a low bar compared to me), it’ll be less of an issue.

Depending on what skin issues or concerns you’re looking to address with your LED face mask, you’ll want to focus on which treatments it offers. This is driven by the color of light the device uses, which dictates its benefits. Some on this list offer multiple services, while others zero in on one. These are the common options:

While some are comfortable and allow for multitasking, there is no getting around the fact that you’re wearing a large light on your face. As a long-time migraine sufferer, having a light this close to my eyes for too long can be a trigger. But even if you’re perfectly fine with prolonged light exposure, you’ll want to know what the time commitment is before buying LED face masks, as they’re most effective when used regularly. Some are as long as 25 minutes, while others can be as short as three minutes. Keep in mind that not all are meant for everyday use; some (especially the ones with longer treatment lengths) may only need to be used a few times a week for max efficiency.

When shopping for an LED face mask, choosing a device that’s FDA-cleared is essential, says Dr. Kopelman. This ensures the product meets fundamental safety standards for consumer use. To be clear, however, FDA-cleared is not the same as FDA-approved—the latter involves extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing. Currently, no LED face masks on the market have achieved FDA approval.

For now, stick with FDA-cleared options, which means the device is proven to be as safe and effective as another legally marketed product. You might also see terms like FDA-registered or FDA-listed, but these simply indicate that the manufacturer has notified the FDA of the product's existence—there’s no review or evaluation involved. Because of that uncertainty, you won’t see any of those on this list.

There are a lot of LED face masks out there, and like any trendy tool, not all are created equal. So, before putting any to the test, I consulted with a panel of dermatologists on which devices were legit and which they recommend. They also advised me on what to look for in a quality LED face mask and the brands to focus on. Based on this intel, I, along with other Men’s Health writers and editors, put several masks to the test, evaluating each device’s effectiveness, ease of use, and how comfortable it was to wear.

As many LED face masks do not offer immediate results, we used each one for at least one month to ensure enough time was given to gain any possible benefits. Following this extensive research and testing, I landed on these seven LED face masks as the best for men in 2026.

The dermatologists I spoke to for this story were clear on this: you should be cleaning your device after every use. If you don’t, bacteria, oil, and product residue can build up on the surface and transfer back onto your skin, causing irritation or breakouts, which may ironically be what you were hoping to minimize by using an LED mask in the first place.

Dr. Kopelman says that LED masks should always be used on freshly cleansed, dry skin to ensure the light penetrates as effectively as possible. After the session, apply your serums and moisturizers—doing it beforehand can block the light and reduce its benefits. A hydrating serum like hyaluronic acid or a peptide-rich cream works especially well to complement the collagen boost from the treatment, Dr. Kopelman says.

According to Dr. Toy, be sure to skip any products that might react to light. For example, because retinol and vitamin C serums are photosensitizing, they’re an absolute no-go before any LED treatment. Dr. Chacon adds that reflective products like heavy oils or sunscreens should also be avoided during use as they can scatter the light and disrupt the device’s effectiveness.

#4575. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with no subscription required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs.
